claim: MEG/EEG non-invasively record human brain activity with millisecond resolution providing reliable markers of healthy and disease states.
source: Magneto- and electro-encephalography (MEG/EEG) non-invasively record human brain activity with millisecond resolution providing reliable markers of healthy and disease states.
evidence: This is a general statement about MEG/EEG capabilities that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Relating macroscopic MEG/EEG signals to underlying cellular- and circuit-level generators is a limitation that constrains using MEG/EEG to reveal novel principles of information processing or to translate findings into new therapies for neuropathology.
source: Relating these macroscopic signals to underlying cellular- and circuit-level generators is a limitation that constrains using MEG/EEG to reveal novel principles of information processing or to translate findings into new therapies for neuropathology.
evidence: This statement reflects the authors' assessment of current limitations in the field based on their knowledge and experience.

claim: HNN has a graphical user interface designed to help researchers and clinicians interpret the neural origins of MEG/EEG.
source: HNN has a graphical user interface designed to help researchers and clinicians interpret the neural origins of MEG/EEG.
evidence: This is a direct description of the software's features.

claim: HNN's core is a neocortical circuit model that accounts for biophysical origins of electrical currents generating MEG/EEG.
source: HNN's core is a neocortical circuit model that accounts for biophysical origins of electrical currents generating MEG/EEG.
evidence: This describes the fundamental architecture of the HNN software.

claim: Data can be directly compared to simulated signals in HNN and parameters easily manipulated to develop/test hypotheses on a signal's origin.
source: Data can be directly compared to simulated signals and parameters easily manipulated to develop/test hypotheses on a signal's origin.
evidence: This describes functionality of the HNN software.

claim: EEG and MEG are the only noninvasive methods to study electrical neural activity in humans with fine temporal resolution.
source: To date, EEG and MEG are the only noninvasive methods to study electrical neural activity in humans with fine temporal resolution.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge in neuroscience about available recording modalities.

claim: EEG/MEG provide biomarkers of almost all healthy and abnormal brain dynamics.
source: Despite the fact that EEG/MEG provide biomarkers of almost all healthy and abnormal brain dynamics, these so called 'macro-scale' techniques suffer from difficulty in interpretability in terms of the underlying cellular- and circuit-level events.
evidence: This is a general statement about the utility of EEG/MEG based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Macro-scale EEG/MEG techniques suffer from difficulty in interpretability in terms of the underlying cellular- and circuit-level events.
source: Despite the fact that EEG/MEG provide biomarkers of almost all healthy and abnormal brain dynamics, these so called 'macro-scale' techniques suffer from difficulty in interpretability in terms of the underlying cellular- and circuit-level events.
evidence: This is an assessment of current limitations in the field based on knowledge and inference.

claim: HNN's underlying neocortical model represents a canonical neocortical circuit based on generalizable features of cortical circuitry.
source: HNN's underlying model represents a canonical neocortical circuit based on generalizable features of cortical circuitry, with individual pyramidal neurons and interneurons arranged across the cortical layers, and layer-specific input pathways that relay spiking information from other parts of the brain, which are not explicitly modeled.
evidence: This describes the design principles of the HNN model.

claim: The elementary current generators of EEG/MEG (current dipoles) are simulated from the intracellular current flow in the long and spatially-aligned pyramidal neuron dendrites.
source: Based on known electromagnetic biophysics underlying macroscale EEG/MEG signals (Jones, 2015), the elementary current generators of EEG/MEG (current dipoles) are simulated from the intracellular current flow in the long and spatially-aligned pyramidal neuron dendrites (Hämäläinen et al., 1993; Ikeda et al., 2005; Jones, 2015; Murakami et al., 2003; Murakami and Okada, 2006; Okada et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work establishing the biophysical basis of EEG/MEG signals.

claim: HNN's construction produces equal units between the model output and source-localized data (ampere-meters, Am) allowing one-to-one comparison between model and data.
source: This unique construction produces equal units between the model output and source-localized data (ampere-meters, Am) allowing one-to-one comparison between model and data to guide interpretation.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the HNN model design.

claim: HNN's underlying mathematical model has been successfully applied to interpret the mechanisms and meaning of sensory evoked responses and oscillations in the alpha (7–14 Hz), beta (15–29 Hz) and gamma bands (30–80 Hz).
source: HNN's underlying mathematical model has been successfully applied to interpret the mechanisms and meaning of these common signals, including sensory evoked responses and oscillations in the alpha (7–14 Hz), beta (15–29 Hz) and gamma bands (30–80 Hz) (Jones et al., 2009; Jones et al., 2007; Lee and Jones, 2013; Sherman et al., 2016; Ziegler et al., 2010), and changes with perception (Jones et al., 2007) and aging (Ziegler et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior publications using the model.

claim: The model has been used to study the impact of non-invasive brain stimulation on circuit dynamics measured with EEG.
source: The model has also been used to study the impact of non-invasive brain stimulation on circuit dynamics measured with EEG (Sliva et al., 2018), and to constrain more reduced 'neural mass models' of laminar activity (Pinotsis et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior publication.

claim: HNN's model has been applied to study MEG-measured circuit deficits in autism.
source: In the clinical domain, HNN's model has also been applied to study MEG-measured circuit deficits in autism (Khan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior publication.

claim: The complexity of the original model and code hindered use by the general community.
source: Despite these examples of use, the complexity of the original model and code hindered use by the general community.
evidence: This is an inference based on the authors' experience with the prior version of the model.

claim: The innovation in the new HNN software is the construction of an intuitive graphical user interface to interact with the model without any coding.
source: The innovation in the new HNN software is the construction of an intuitive graphical user interface to interact with the model without any coding.
evidence: This describes the key innovation of the HNN software.

claim: HNN is constructed to be a hypothesis development and testing tool to produce circuit-level predictions that can then be directly tested and informed by invasive recordings and/or other imaging modalities.
source: HNN is constructed to be a hypothesis development and testing tool to produce circuit-level predictions that can then be directly tested and informed by invasive recordings and/or other imaging modalities.
evidence: This describes the intended purpose and design of HNN.

claim: MEG and EEG are ultimately generated by the primary currents.
source: As depicted in Figure 1, both MEG and EEG are ultimately generated by the primary currents.
evidence: This is based on established electromagnetic biophysics and is illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The primary currents set up a potential distribution (V) that extends through the brain tissue, the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), the skull, and the scalp, where it is measured as EEG.
source: The primary currents set up a potential distribution (V) that extends through the brain tissue, the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), the skull, and the scalp, where it is measured as EEG; the passive JV is proportional to the electric field (negative gradient of V) and electrical conductivity (σ).
evidence: This describes the biophysical basis of EEG generation based on established knowledge.

claim: MEG is generated by both the primary current (Jp) and volume current (Jv).
source: MEG, in general, is generated by both the Jp and Jv.
evidence: This is based on established electromagnetic biophysics.

claim: The direction of the primary current is determined by the cellular level geometry of the active cells.
source: Furthermore, the direction of the primary current is determined by the cellular level geometry of the active cells.
evidence: This is based on established biophysical principles.

claim: A spherically symmetric conductor model can often be used for MEG forward modeling.
source: Specifically, a first order approximation, the spherically symmetric conductor model (Sarvas, 1987), can often be used (Tarkiainen et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on MEG forward modeling.

claim: In a spherically symmetric conductor model, all components of the magnetic field can be computed from an analytical formula which is independent of the value of the electrical conductivity as a function of the distance from the center of the sphere.
source: In this case, all components of the magnetic field can be computed from an analytical formula which is independent of the value of the electrical conductivity as a function of the distance from the center of the sphere (Sarvas, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The inverse problem of estimating primary current activity from MEG and EEG sensor data is fundamentally ill-posed.
source: However, this inverse problem is fundamentally ill-posed, and constraints are needed to render the problem unique.
evidence: This is a well-established principle in EEG/MEG source estimation.

claim: The appropriate elementary primary current source in all source estimation methods is estimated as a current dipole, with units current x distance, that is Am (Ampere x meter).
source: Importantly, due to physiological considerations, the appropriate elementary primary current source in all of these methods is estimated as a current dipole, with units current x distance, that is Am (Ampere x meter).
evidence: This is based on established biophysical principles.

claim: The primary current is oriented normal to the cortical mantle and its direction corresponds to the intracellular current flow.
source: Thanks to the consistent orientation of the apical dendrites of the pyramidal cells in the cortex this primary current is oriented normal to the cortical mantle and its direction corresponds to the intracellular current flow (Okada et al., 1997; Ikeda et al., 2005; Murakami and Okada, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work on the biophysical basis of EEG/MEG.

claim: HNN simulates the primary current from a canonical model of a layered neocortical column via the net intracellular electrical current flow in the pyramidal neuron dendrites in a direction parallel to the apical dendrites.
source: Specifically, HNN simulates the primary current from a canonical model of a layered neocortical column via the net intracellular electrical current flow in the pyramidal neuron dendrites in a direction parallel to the apical dendrites (see red arrow in Figures 1 and 2, and further discussion in Materials and methods) (Hämäläinen et al., 1993; Ikeda et al., 2005; Jones, 2015; Murakami et al., 2003; Murakami and Okada, 2006; Okada et al., 1997).
evidence: This describes how HNN simulates primary currents and is supported by citations and figures.

claim: The units of measure produced by the HNN model are the same as those estimated from source localization methods, namely, ampere-meters (Am).
source: With this construction, the units of measure produced by the model are the same as those estimated from source localization methods, namely, ampere-meters (Am), enabling one-to-one comparison of results.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the HNN model design.

claim: HNN is currently constructed to dissect the cell and network contributions to signals from one source-localized region of interest.
source: HNN is currently constructed to dissect the cell and network contributions to signals from one source-localized region of interest.
evidence: This describes the current scope of HNN.

claim: HNN's underlying neocortical network represents a scalable patch of neocortex containing canonical features of neocortical circuitry.
source: As such, HNN's underlying neocortical network represents a scalable patch of neocortex containing canonical features of neocortical circuitry (Figure 2).
evidence: This describes the design of HNN's network model and is illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: The primary electrical current that generates EEG/MEG signals comes from synchronous activity in pyramidal neuron (PN) dendrites across a large population.
source: Given that the primary electrical current that generates EEG/MEG signals comes from synchronous activity in pyramidal neuron (PN) dendrites across a large population, there are several key features of neocortical circuitry that are essential to consider when simulating these currents.
evidence: This is based on established biophysical principles of EEG/MEG generation.

claim: Many features of neocortical circuits are remarkably similar across cortical areas and species.
source: While there are known differences in microscale circuitry across cortical areas and species, many features of neocortical circuits are remarkably similar.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in neuroscience.

claim: Conserved features of neocortical circuits are minimally sufficient to account for the generation of evoked responses and brain rhythms measured with EEG/MEG.
source: We assume these conserved features are minimally sufficient to account for the generation of evoked responses and brain rhythms measured with EEG/MEG, and we have harnessed this generalization into HNN's foundational model, with success in simulating many of these signals using the same template model (see Introduction).
evidence: This is an assumption underlying the HNN model design, supported by inference from prior successful applications.

claim: HNN's template circuit includes a 3-layered structure with pyramidal neurons in the supragranular and infragranular layers whose dendrites span across the layers and are synaptically coupled to inhibitory interneurons in a 3-to-1 ratio of pyramidal to inhibitory cells.
source: A 3-layered structure with pyramidal neurons in the supragranular and infragranular layers whose dendrites span across the layers and are synaptically coupled to inhibitory interneurons in a 3-to-1 ratio of pyramidal to inhibitory cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: This describes the structure of HNN's template circuit and is illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: Cells in the granular layer are not explicitly included in the template circuit.
source: Of note, cells in the granular layer are not explicitly included in the template circuit.
evidence: This describes a design choice in the HNN model.

claim: Macroscale current dipoles are dominated by PN activity in supragranular and infragranular layers.
source: This initial design choice was based on the fact that macroscale current dipoles are dominated by PN activity in supragranular and infragranular layers.
evidence: This is based on established biophysical principles and justifies a design choice in HNN.

claim: Thalamic input to granular layers is presumed to propagate directly to basal and oblique dendrites of PN in the supragranular and infragranular layers.
source: Thalamic input to granular layers is presumed to propagate directly to basal and oblique dendrites of PN in the supragranular and infragranular layers.
evidence: This is an assumption in the HNN model based on knowledge of cortical circuitry.

claim: The number of cells in the HNN network is adjustable while maintaining a 3-to-1 pyramidal to inhibitory interneuron ratio in each layer.
source: The number of cells in the network is adjustable in the Local Network Parameters window via the Cells tab, while maintaining at 3-to-1 pyramidal to inhibitory interneuron ratio in each layer.
evidence: This describes a feature of the HNN software.

claim: Evoked responses are typically on the order of 10 – 100nAm, and are estimated to be generated by the synchronous spiking activity of the order of tens of thousands of pyramidal neurons.
source: Evoked responses are typically on the order of 10 – 100nAm, and are estimated to be generated by the synchronous spiking activity of the order of tens of thousands of pyramidal neurons.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge and estimates in the field.

claim: Low-frequency oscillations are larger in magnitude and are on the order of 100–1000 nAm, and are estimated to be generated by the subthreshold activity of on the order of a million pyramidal neurons.
source: Low-frequency oscillations are larger in magnitude and are on the order of 100–1000 nAm, and are estimated to be generated by the subthreshold activity of on the order of a million pyramidal neurons (Jones et al., 2009; Jones et al., 2007; Murakami and Okada, 2006).
evidence: This is based on prior work cited.

claim: One type of input to HNN's model represents excitatory synaptic drive that comes from the lemniscal thalamus and contacts the cortex in the granular layers, which then propagates to the proximal PN dendrites in the supragranular and infragranular layers and somata of the inhibitory neurons; this input is referred to as proximal drive.
source: One type of input represents excitatory synaptic drive that comes from the lemniscal thalamus and contacts the cortex in the granular layers, which then propagates to the proximal PN dendrites in the supragranular and infragranular layers and somata of the inhibitory neurons; this input is referred to as proximal drive (Figure 3B).
evidence: This describes a feature of the HNN model and is illustrated in Figure 3B.

claim: Another input to HNN's model represents excitatory synaptic drive from higher-order cortex or non-specific thalamic nuclei that synapses directly into the supragranular layers and contacts the distal PN dendrites and somata of the inhibitory neuron; this input is referred to as distal drive.
source: The other input represents excitatory synaptic drive from higher-order cortex or non-specific thalamic nuclei that synapses directly into the supragranular layers and contacts the distal PN dendrites and somata of the inhibitory neuron; this input is referred to as distal drive (Figure 3C).
evidence: This describes a feature of the HNN model and is illustrated in Figure 3C.

claim: The networks that provide proximal and distal input to the local circuit are not explicitly modelled, but rather these inputs are represented by simulated trains of action potentials that activate excitatory post-synaptic receptors in the local network.
source: The networks that provide proximal and distal input to the local circuit (e.g., thalamus and higher order cortex) are not explicitly modelled, but rather these inputs are represented by simulated trains of action potentials that activate excitatory post-synaptic receptors in the local network.
evidence: This describes a design choice in the HNN model.

claim: The timing and the strength of the exogenous drive to the local network were the only parameters that were originally tuned to simulate ERPs and oscillations.
source: All of these equations and parameters were then fixed, and the only parameters that were originally tuned to simulate ERPs and oscillations were the timing and the strength of the exogenous drive to the local network.
evidence: This describes the parameter tuning approach used in developing HNN.

claim: The biophysical constraints on the origin of the current dipoles signal will dictate the output of the model and necessarily limit the space of parameter adjustments that can accurately account for the recorded data.
source: Importantly, the biophysical constraints on the origin of the current dipoles signal (discussed above) will dictate the output of the model and necessarily limit the space of parameter adjustments that can accurately account for the recorded data.
evidence: This is an inference about how biophysical constraints affect model behavior.

claim: A parameter sensitivity analysis on perturbations around the default ERP parameter sets confirmed that a subset of the parameters have the strongest influence on features of the ERP waveform.
source: A parameter sensitivity analysis on perturbations around the default ERP parameter sets confirmed that a subset of the parameters have the strongest influence on features of the ERP waveform (see Supplementary Materials).
evidence: This is supported by data from sensitivity analysis presented in supplementary materials.

claim: HNN's interactive GUI is designed for users with no formal computational neural modeling or software development experience to be able to develop and test hypotheses on the cellular- and circuit-level generators of their human data.
source: HNN's interactive GUI is designed for users with no formal computational neural modeling or software development experience to be able to develop and test hypotheses on the cellular- and circuit-level generators of their human data.
evidence: This describes the design goal of HNN.

claim: The template network model contains features of a canonical neocortical circuit, with layer-specific thalamocortical and cortico-cortical drive, where the net primary current dipoles are simulated from the intracellular current across the network of pyramidal neurons.
source: The template network model contains features of a canonical neocortical circuit, with layer-specific thalamocortical and cortico-cortical drive, where the net primary current dipoles are simulated from the intracellular current across the network of pyramidal neurons.
evidence: This describes the structure of HNN's template model.

claim: HNN led to a novel prediction on the origin of transient neocortical beta oscillations, and the prediction was later tested and supported by laminar recordings in mice and monkeys.
source: As one specific example, HNN led to a novel prediction on the origin of transient neocortical beta oscillations, and the prediction was later tested and supported by laminar recordings in mice and monkeys (Sherman et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior publication that validated model predictions.

claim: The scalability of HNN provides an unprecedented framework for translational neuroscience research.
source: Overall, the scalability of HNN provides an unprecedented framework for translational neuroscience research.
evidence: This is a claim about the utility of HNN based on inference from its design features.

claim: HNN's model is unique compared to other EEG/MEG modeling software.
source: This construction is unique compared to other EEG/MEG modeling software (see Discussion).
evidence: This is a comparative claim that is elaborated in the Discussion section.

claim: The tactile evoked response could be reproduced in HNN by 'activating' the network with a sequence of layer-specific proximal and distal spike train drive to the local network.
source: In prior publications, we showed that this tactile evoked response could be reproduced in HNN by 'activating' the network with a sequence of layer-specific proximal and distal spike train drive to the local network, which is distributed with HNN in the file 'ERPYes100Trials.param'.
evidence: This is based on prior published work and data included with HNN.

claim: The sequence of drive that accurately reproduced the tactile evoked response consisted of 'feedforward'/proximal input at ~25 ms post stimulus, followed by 'feedback'/distal input at ~60 ms, followed by a subsequent 'feedforward'/proximal input at ~125 ms.
source: The drive sequence that accurately reproduced the tactile evoked response consisted of 'feedforward'/proximal input at ~25 ms post stimulus, followed by 'feedback'/distal input at ~60 ms, followed by a subsequent 'feedforward'/proximal input at ~125 ms (Gaussian distribution of input times on each simulated trial, Figure 4C).
evidence: This describes the specific drive sequence used to reproduce the evoked response and is illustrated in Figure 4C.

claim: A scaling factor was applied to net dipole output to match to the magnitude of the recorded ERP data and used to predict the number of neurons contributing to the recorded ERP.
source: Note, a scaling factor was applied to net dipole output to match to the magnitude of the recorded ERP data and used to predict the number of neurons contributing to the recorded ERP.
evidence: This describes a method used in HNN to relate model output to data.

claim: In the tactile evoked response example, 600,000 neurons contributed to the evoked response.
source: In this case, since there are 100 pyramidal neurons in each of layers 2/3 and 5, that amounts to 600,000 neurons (200 neurons x 3000 scaling factor) contributing to the evoked response, consistent with the experimental literature (described in Jones et al., 2009 and Jones et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a calculation based on the scaling factor applied in the model and is consistent with cited literature.

claim: Alpha rhythms in neocortex rely on ~10 Hz bursting in the thalamus.
source: Motivated by a long history of research showing alpha rhythms in neocortex rely on ~10 Hz bursting in the thalamus, we tested the hypothesis that ~10 Hz bursts of drive through proximal and distal projection pathways (representing lemniscal and non-lemniscal thalamic drive) could reproduce an alpha rhythm in the local circuit.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: When ~ 10 Hz bursts of proximal and distal drives are subthreshold and arrive to the local network in anti-phase (~50 ms delay) a pure alpha rhythm emerges.
source: We showed that when ~ 10 Hz bursts of proximal and distal drives are subthreshold and arrive to the local network in anti-phase (~50 ms delay) a pure alpha rhythm emerges (Jones et al., 2009; Ziegler et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior publications.

claim: Brief bouts of beta activity ('beta events') non-time locked to alpha events could be generated by decreasing the mean delay between the proximal and distal drive to 0 ms and increasing the strength of the distal drive relative to the proximal drive.
source: By hand tuning the parameters we were able to match the output of the model to several features of the recorded data, including symmetric amplitude modulation around zero and PSD plots as shown in Figures 7 and 8 (see further feature matching in Jones et al., 2009 and Sherman et al., 2016), we arrived at the hypothesis that brief bouts of beta activity ('beta events') non-time locked to alpha events could be generated by decreasing the mean delay between the proximal and distal drive to 0 ms and increasing the strength of the distal drive relative to the proximal drive.
evidence: This is a hypothesis developed through model tuning and is illustrated in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: Beta events emerge on cycles when the two stochastic drives hit the network simultaneously and when the distal drive is strong enough to break the upward flowing current and create a prominent ~50 ms downward deflection.
source: With this mechanism, beta events emerged on cycles when the two stochastic drives hit the network simultaneously and when the distal drive was strong enough to break the upward flowing current and create a prominent ~50 ms downward deflection (see red box in Figure 8B).
evidence: This describes the mechanism of beta event generation in the model and is illustrated in Figure 8B.

claim: The beta event hypothesis was purely model derived and was based on matching several features of the SI mu rhythm between the model output and data.
source: This beta event hypothesis was purely model derived and was based on matching several features of the SI mu rhythm between the model output and data (detailed in Jones et al., 2009 Sherman et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the origin of the beta event hypothesis and is supported by citations.

claim: Model derived predictions on mechanisms underlying alpha and beta were motivated by literature and further refined by tuning the parameters to match the output of the model with various features of the recorded data.
source: The model derived predictions on mechanisms underlying alpha and beta where motivated by literature and further refined by tuning the parameters to match the output of the model with various features of the recorded data.
evidence: This describes the process used to develop predictions with HNN.

claim: One specific prediction was that the orientation of the current during the prominent ~50 ms deflection defining a beta event was down the pyramidal neuron dendrites (e.g. into the cortex).
source: One specific prediction was that the orientation of the current during the prominent ~50 ms deflection defining a beta event (red box, Figure 8B) was down the pyramidal neuron dendrites (e.g. into the cortex).
evidence: This is a specific prediction from the model illustrated in Figure 8B.

claim: Predictions on beta events were subsequently tested and validated with laminar recordings in both mice and monkeys, where it was also confirmed that features of beta events are conserved across species and recording modalities.
source: This prediction, along with several others, were subsequently tested and validated with laminar recordings in both mice and monkeys, where it was also confirmed that features of beta events are conserved across species and recording modalities (Sherman et al., 2016; Shin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to publications that validated model predictions.

claim: Low gamma rhythms in the 30–80 Hz range can emerge in local spiking networks through excitatory and inhibitory cell interactions where synaptic time constants set the frequency of the oscillation.
source: It has been well established through experiments and computational modeling that these rhythms can emerge in local spiking networks through excitatory and inhibitory cell interactions where synaptic time constants set the frequency of the oscillation, while broadband or 'high gamma' rhythms reflect spiking activity in the network that creates sharp waveform deflections (Lee and Jones, 2013).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge and is supported by citation.

claim: The period of the low gamma oscillation is determined by the time constant of decay of GABAA-mediated inhibitory currents.
source: The period of the low gamma oscillation is determined by the time constant of decay of GABAA-mediated inhibitory currents (Buzsáki and Wang, 2012; Cardin et al., 2009; Vierling-Claassen et al., 2010), a mechanism that has been referred to as pyramidal-interneuron gamma (PING).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on gamma oscillations.

claim: In normal regimes, the decay time constant of GABAA-mediated synapses (~25 ms) bounds oscillations to the low gamma frequency band (~40 Hz).
source: In normal regimes, the decay time constant of GABAA-mediated synapses (~25 ms) bounds oscillations to the low gamma frequency band (~40 Hz).
evidence: This is based on established biophysical principles.

claim: PING rhythms are initiated by 'excitation' to the excitatory (PN) cells, and this initial excitation causes PN spiking that, in turn, synaptically activates a spiking population of inhibitory (I) cells.
source: In general, PING rhythms are initiated by 'excitation' to the excitatory (PN) cells, and this initial excitation causes PN spiking that, in turn, synaptically activates a spiking population of inhibitory (I) cells.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of PING rhythms based on established knowledge.

claim: HNN was applied to determine if features in the current dipole signal could distinguish PING-mediated gamma from other possible mechanisms such as exogenous rhythmic drive or spiking activity that creates 'high gamma' oscillations.
source: We have applied HNN to determine if features in the current dipole signal could distinguish PING-mediated gamma from other possible mechanisms such as exogenous rhythmic drive or spiking activity that creates 'high gamma' oscillations (Lee and Jones, 2013).
evidence: This describes an application of HNN and is supported by citation.

claim: To improve the fit to the suprathreshold evoked response data, a procedure for sequentially optimizing the strengths of the proximal and distal drive inputs generating the evoked response can be run.
source: To improve the fit to the data, a procedure for sequentially optimizing the strengths of the proximal and distal drive inputs generating the evoked response can be run.
evidence: This describes a feature of HNN's optimization procedure.

claim: The RMSE between the data and the model improved from 30.53 to 15.54 after optimization for the suprathreshold evoked response.
source: Here, the simulation from the optimized parameter set for the suprathreshold evoked response is shown in gray with an improved RMSE of 15.54 compared to 30.53 for the initial model.
evidence: This is data from the optimization example shown in Figure 11.

claim: HNN is a neural modeling software tool developed to help researchers and clinicians interpret the neural origin of their human EEG or MEG data.
source: The Human Neocortical Neurosolver (HNN, https://hnn.brown.edu) is a neural modeling software tool developed to help researchers and clinicians interpret the neural origin of their human EEG or MEG data.
evidence: This is a summary statement about HNN.

claim: The tutorials and the example workflow focus on studying the neural origin of ERPs and low-frequency oscillations from a single brain region.
source: Based on prior applications of HNN's underlying template neural model on these signals (Jones et al., 2009; Jones et al., 2007; Khan et al., 2015; Lee and Jones, 2013; Sherman et al., 2016; Sliva et al., 2018; Ziegler et al., 2010), the tutorials and the example workflow focus on studying the neural origin of ERPs and low-frequency oscillations from a single brain region.
evidence: This describes the focus of HNN's tutorials and is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: HNN enables visualization and direct comparison of the primary current dipole produced by the network to source-localized data in units of Am, under various parameter manipulations.
source: HNN enables visualization and direct comparison of the primary current dipole produced by the network to source-localized data in units of Am, under various parameter manipulations.
evidence: This describes a key feature of HNN.

claim: HNN was created based on the biophysical origin of EEG/MEG primary currents to be a hypothesis development and testing tool.
source: HNN was created based on the biophysical origin of EEG/MEG primary currents to be a hypothesis development and testing tool, where specific predictions on the microcircuit-level underpinnings of recorded data can be produced.
evidence: This describes the design philosophy of HNN.

claim: The circuit-level predictions from HNN can guide further validation with invasive recordings or with other imaging modalities.
source: The circuit-level predictions can guide further validation with invasive recordings or with other imaging modalities (e.g., spectroscopy or tractography, see Khan et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the intended use of HNN and is supported by citation to an example.

claim: HNN is particularly timely given the rapidly expanding wealth of genetic insights and phenotype data in animal model systems.
source: HNN is particularly timely given the rapidly expanding wealth of genetic insights and phenotype data in animal model systems.
evidence: This is an assessment of the timeliness of HNN based on current trends in neuroscience.

claim: As disease-specific genetic mutations and corresponding cellular/circuit outcomes in mouse models are identified, they can be implemented in HNN, and their impact on EEG/MEG measured brain dynamics can be simulated.
source: As disease-specific genetic mutations and corresponding cellular/circuit outcomes in mouse models are identified, they can be implemented in HNN, and their impact on EEG/MEG measured brain dynamics, ranging from ongoing state properties (e.g., alpha oscillations) to sensory-evoked responses, can be simulated.
evidence: This describes a potential application of HNN based on speculation about future use.

claim: Among current modeling software designed specifically for study of EEG/MEG signals, HNN's model, goals, and capabilities are unique.
source: Among the current modeling software designed specifically for study of EEG/MEG signals (e.g., The Virtual Brain [TVB] https://thevirtualbrain.org, Dynamic Causal Modeling [DCM] of E/MEG within the Statistical Parametric Mapping [SPM] software https://www.fil.ion.ucl.ac.uk/spm/, and LFPy https://lfpy.readthedocs.io/en/latest/; Hagen et al., 2018; Kiebel et al., 2008; Sanz Leon et al., 2013), HNN's model, goals, and capabilities are unique.
evidence: This is a comparative claim about HNN relative to other software.

claim: The goal of HNN is to provide a user-friendly graphical interface to a validated biophysically detailed model of neocortical circuitry, and to teach the community, regardless of neural modeling or coding experience, how to interact with the model to study the neural origin of commonly measured macroscale EEG/MEG signals.

source: HNN's model is simulated across multiple cores in parallel using the message-passing interface (MPI).

source: The morphology of the PN in each layer (see Figure 3, and Table 1) were adapted from the morphology reduction procedure in Bush and Sejnowski (1993).
evidence: This describes the source of the neuron morphology in HNN and is supported by citation.

claim: In Bush and Sejnowski (1993), digitized HRP-filled pyramidal neurons from layers 2 and 5 of cat visual cortex consisting of 400 compartments were reduced to 8 and 9 compartments, respectively.
source: In Bush and Sejnowski (1993), digitized HRP-filled pyramidal neurons from layers 2 and 5 of cat visual cortex consisting of 400 compartments were reduced to 8 and 9 compartments, respectively.
evidence: This describes the morphology reduction procedure from a cited source.

claim: In HNN, a scaling factor of 1.3 was applied to the length and diameters of the dendritic compartments to account for increases in dendritic length and volume in human somatosensory neurons.
source: In HNN, a scaling factor of 1.3 was applied to the length and diameters of the dendritic compartments to account for increases in dendritic length and volume in human somatosensory neurons, as predicted by larger cortical thickness (Fischl and Dale, 2000; Geyer et al., 1997) and an increase in the number of dendritic spines and arborization (Elston et al., 2001).
evidence: This describes a modification made in HNN and is supported by citations.

claim: Membrane voltages in each simulated compartment were calculated using the standard Hodgkin-Huxley parallel conductance equations.
source: Membrane voltages in each simulated compartment were calculated using the standard Hodgkin-Huxley parallel conductance equations, and current flow between compartments follows from cable theory as accounted for in NEURON.
evidence: This describes the biophysical equations used in HNN.

claim: Active ionic currents were included in both the somatic and dendritic compartment of the cells of the pyramidal neurons, and in the single compartment of the inhibitory neurons.
source: Extending the prior work of Bush and Sejnowski (1993), active ionic currents were included in both the somatic and dendritic compartment of the cells of the pyramidal neurons, and in the single compartment of the inhibitory neurons.
evidence: This describes the biophysical detail in HNN's model.

claim: The maximal conductances of each current were constant throughout the soma and dendrite.
source: The maximal conductances of each current were constant throughout the soma and dendrite (Bekkers, 2000; Korngreen and Sakmann, 2000; Migliore and Shepherd, 2002; Stuart and Sakmann, 1994) and were chosen to produce adapting spikes in the L2/3 PNs and bursting in the L5 PNs to current injected in the soma (1 nA for 100 ms) representative of neurons classified as regular spiking and intrinsically bursting, respectively (Moore and Nelson, 1998; Silva et al., 1991; Zhu and Connors, 1999).
evidence: This describes parameter choices in HNN's model and is supported by citations.

claim: The inhibitory neurons were tuned to represent basket cells and produced regular fast spiking dynamics to injected current.
source: The inhibitory neurons were tuned to represent basket cells and produced regular fast spiking dynamics to injected current, as in other cortical network models (Garabedian et al., 2003; Jones et al., 2000; Pinto et al., 2003).
evidence: This describes the tuning of inhibitory neurons in HNN and is supported by citations.

source: HNN's default template neocortical model includes neurons arranged in three dimensions. The XY plane is used to array cells on a regular grid while the Z-axis specifies cortical layer.
evidence: This describes the spatial organization of HNN's model.

source: HNN's default model contains a regular 10 × 10 grid (arbitrary units) of pyramidal neurons in layer 2/3 and layer five for a total of 200 pyramidal neurons, with interneurons interleaved regularly in a 3–1 ratio (see Figure 3D).

claim: The local synaptic architecture in HNN was based on an abundance of animal studies and, in particular, studies of the mouse/rat somatosensory cortex.
source: The local synaptic architecture in Figure 3A was based on an abundance of animal studies and, in particular, studies of the mouse/rat somatosensory cortex (Bernardo et al., 1990a; Bernardo et al., 1990b; for review, see Thomson et al., 2002; Thomson and Bannister, 2003, and Bannister, 2005).
evidence: This describes the basis for HNN's connectivity and is supported by citations.

claim: Inhibitory synaptic connections onto PNs were located on the soma.
source: Inhibitory synaptic connections onto PNs were located on the soma (Freund et al., 1986; Kisvárday et al., 1985; Somogyi et al., 1983), and excitatory synapses contacted the basal and apical oblique dendrites (Deuchars et al., 1994; Feldmeyer et al., 2002; Lübke et al., 1996; Thomson and Bannister, 1998).
evidence: This describes synaptic connectivity in HNN and is supported by citations.

claim: Synaptic dynamics were modeled with bi-exponential functions.
source: Synaptic dynamics were modeled with bi-exponential functions.
evidence: This describes the mathematical representation of synapses in HNN.

claim: There is all-to-all connectivity between any two populations of synaptically-coupled neurons in HNN.
source: There is all-to-all connectivity between any two populations of synaptically-coupled neurons.
evidence: This describes the connectivity pattern in HNN's model.

claim: Axial current flow between any two neighboring model compartments i,j is defined as iaxial = (vi - vj)/raxial.
source: Axial current flow between any two neighboring model compartments i,j is defined as iaxial = (vi - vj)/raxial, where vi, vj, and raxial are the voltages in compartment i, j, and the resistance between the compartments, respectively.
evidence: This describes the calculation of axial current in HNN.

claim: To convert axial current into a dipole signal, a length scaling is applied where the axial current is scaled by the inter-compartment distance along the vertical axis.
source: In order to convert this axial current into a dipole signal, we apply a length scaling where the axial current is scaled by the inter-compartment distance along the vertical axis.
evidence: This describes the method for calculating dipole signals in HNN.

claim: The contribution from all neighboring compartments within a neuron is integrated and then added to a value across the set of all pyramidal neurons to produce the model dipole output signal.
source: The contribution from all neighboring compartments within a neuron is integrated and then added to a value across the set of all pyramidal neurons.
evidence: This describes how the net dipole is calculated in HNN.

claim: As a result of the multiplication between axial current and length, the model dipole output signal has the same units of measure as the experimental data (Am).
source: As a result of the multiplication between axial current and length, the model dipole output signal has the same units of measure as the experimental data (Am) (Okada et al., 1997; Murakami et al., 2003; Murakami and Okada, 2006; Jones et al., 2007; Hagen et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes a key feature of HNN's output and is supported by citations.

source: HNN includes a method to optimize ERP simulations. The optimization procedure was uniquely designed to minimize the RMSE between model output and ERP waveforms in a stepwise manner that decreases parameter exploration and saves compute time.

claim: The optimization procedure takes advantage of the assumption that the exogenous proximal and distal driving inputs are essential parameters to tune to get an accurate representation of an ERP waveform.
source: This procedure takes advantage of the assumption that the exogenous proximal and distal driving inputs are essential parameters to tune to get an accurate representation of an ERP waveform.

evidence: This is a logical inference about temporal causality in the model.

claim: For each optimization step, HNN uses the COBYLA optimization algorithm which supports bound constraints as defined by the user for each parameter.
source: For each optimization step, HNN uses the COBYLA optimization algorithm (Powell, 1994), which supports bound constraints as defined by the user for each parameter.
